criteria.name: Introduction: mission concept and rationale. Include the following required information: What is the spacecraft's primary mission? Why is the mission needed? How many spacecraft are used and why? Who are the users (operator and customers)?
criteria.reasoning: Mission need, rationale, spacecraft count and users are all clearly and specifically addressed, with appropriate literature citations and a convincing Australian-benefit framing.

evidence.quote: The primary mission of ZYZZsat is to image the whole Great Barrier Reef in visible bands at 5 m resolution
One satellite is therefore used. This also simplifies communications, reduces cost, and requires less time to build and launch.
The operator is the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS)
The customers are the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority

criteria.name: Main body: mission design. Present a summary of the mission design using software and/or hand calculations as appropriate. criteria.reasoning: All major design elements are covered with STK screenshots, access data and hand calculations. Some technical weaknesses remain, notably the optimistic revisit calculation and missing link budget/ground-segment verification, so not top of level.

evidence.quote: This report presents the design of ZYZZsat (Z-axis/Y-axis Zeroed Zoning Satellite), a single Earth observation microsatellite for monitoring coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef.

requirements.where: 2.3 Orbit; 2.4 Ground Control & Communications; Appendix A

technical_issues.issue: Revisit calculation divides 2,698 km track spacing by the full 560 km roll-swath width to give about 5 days. The daily track shift is only about 134 km at the equator and the half-swath is about 280 km, so maximum revisit is likely longer (order 8–20 days depending target). The 5-day claim is optimistic.

No X-band link budget is provided, and the design assumes S-band/X-band equipment can be added to the Mount Pleasant 12 m radio telescope. This is an unverified ground-segment implementation assumption and a gap in communications design.

The statement that existing satellite products/depths are mapped at 100 m/pixel conflates a bathymetry model [3] with satellite imagery; the rationale should distinguish bathymetric mapping from satellite remote sensing.

The design assumes rideshare release directly into the 600 km, 97.79° operational orbit, while also noting a possible lower release. A lower release would require a different SSO inclination and likely orbit trim, which is not designed.
Passes are described as 'three in evening and three in morning (UTC)', but the UTC times correspond to evening/morning in Hobart local time, not UTC; the wording is misleading.

overall: Strong, well-structured mission design with all major elements and good STK/hand-calculation support. Main weaknesses are the optimistic revisit-time calculation, no link budget/ground-segment verification, and minor rationale/labelling issues. STK files are listed but only externally referenced, so provision is partly verifiable.

feedback.summary: Overall, this is a strong, well-structured mission design. You address all major elements and support them with STK screenshots, access data and hand calculations. The main improvements are the optimistic revisit calculation, missing X-band link budget/ground-segment verification, the rideshare release-orbit assumption, and Table 5 UTC/local wording. Embedding the STK files will make your evidence fully verifiable.
next_steps: Revise Section 2.3: use the ~134 km daily equatorial track shift and ~280 km half-swath rather than dividing 2,698 km by 560 km; report a realistic maximum revisit (order 8-20 days) or justify the 5-day claim with target-specific access results.

Add an X-band link budget in Section 2.4 and verify the Mount Pleasant 12 m ground-segment modification; correct Table 5's UTC/local-time wording and clarify the rideshare release orbit/trim in Section 2.2.
Make the STK evidence fully verifiable by embedding key screenshots and including the software files in Appendix A, and refine the Introduction's bathymetry-versus-satellite-imagery rationale.

To move toward the top of Accomplished, sharpen the rationale by distinguishing bathymetric mapping [3] from satellite imagery rather than conflating them at 100 m/pixel.

To move toward the top of Accomplished, explicitly link each limitation to the affected design choice and state the next verification step, so the conclusion reads as a clear evidence-based close rather than a list.
